summary: Recommends a minimal set of transport services that end systems should offer and gives guidance on choosing among available mechanisms and protocols. It builds on the transport features in RFC 8303. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs need ways to send data, but there are many possible options. This document picks a small set of basic abilities that a good transport system should offer, and how to choose among them.

questions: what transport services should end systems provide
what is the minimal set of transport services
how can an application request specific transport features
what protocols can implement the minimal set
subtitle: What transport capabilities should applications be able to request

tldr.problem: Applications today mostly use TCP and UDP, which limits the network stack from using features of other protocols. Different transport protocols offer different features, but applications cannot easily switch between them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8923 identifies the essential transport features that all end systems should expose through a common interface, allowing applications to request capabilities without being locked into a specific protocol.
tldr.outcome: Systems that offer this minimal set can implement connections over TCP, UDP, SCTP, or MPTCP, and can switch between them based on application needs, improving flexibility and performance.

today: RFC 8923 is an Informational document from October 2020 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It serves as a guide for the Transport Services (TAPS) Working Group's API design and is used by implementers building transport abstractions that work across multiple protocols.

sections.title: Why a Minimal Set of Transport Services
sections.content:
Transport protocols like TCP, UDP, SCTP, and Multipath TCP offer different features. TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery; UDP is lightweight and datagram-based; SCTP offers multi-streaming and partial reliability. However, most applications are hardcoded to use TCP or UDP, which prevents the system from choosing the best protocol for a particular task.

This RFC recommends a minimal set of transport services that all end systems should expose through a common interface. Applications that request features through this interface can work with any protocol that supports those features, allowing the system to choose TCP, UDP, SCTP, Multipath TCP, or other protocols as appropriate.

The minimal set is designed to be implementable over both TCP and UDP, with limited features, so that even conservative systems can support it. For applications with more advanced needs, the full reduced set in Section 4 is available.
sections.plainLanguage: If a program can say what it needs instead of saying which tool to use, the system can pick the best tool from several choices.

sections.title: Deriving the Minimal Set
sections.content:
The RFC uses a systematic approach to identify which transport features are essential and which can be hidden from applications. It categorizes features into three types: Functional features (the application must know about them to avoid failing, like message ordering), Optimizing features (improve performance but do not affect correctness, like disabling Nagle's algorithm), and Automatable features (the system can handle them on its own without application input, like choosing which IP interface to use).

The minimal set excludes automatable features, which allows the system more freedom to optimize automatically. It also excludes features that cannot be implemented over both TCP and UDP, ensuring broad compatibility.

The RFC then discusses special cases that arise from this reduction. For example, TCP sends and receives bytes, while UDP sends and receives messages. To bridge this gap, the RFC introduces the concept of an Application-Framed Byte Stream (AFra Byte Stream), where senders can optionally mark message boundaries and properties, but receivers only see a stream of bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: To build a universal interface, you start with all possible features, remove those the system can handle automatically, remove those that only work on one protocol, and then solve the weird cases that remain.

sections.title: Organizing Connections and Groups
sections.content:
The minimal set introduces two key concepts for organizing connections. A connection is the shared state between two endpoints and can represent either a transport protocol connection (like a TCP connection) or a stream within a multi-streaming protocol association (like a stream in an SCTP association).

A connection group is a set of connections that share configuration. This allows the system to expose stream scheduling and priority features from protocols like SCTP while remaining compatible with TCP and UDP, which do not have native multi-streaming. In practice, if a system uses TCP it will manage multiple connections independently, but if it uses SCTP it might implement grouped connections as streams in a single association.

The RFC provides a decision tree to help systems choose which transport protocol to use based on application requirements: if reliability or ordering is needed, use TCP or SCTP; if multi-streaming priorities matter, prefer SCTP; if checksum coverage control is needed, UDP-Lite is an option; if nothing special is needed, UDP is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Connections can be grouped so they share settings. If you have multiple conversations that should have the same timeout or priority, grouping them lets the system make smart choices about how to actually send them.

sections.title: The Minimal Set of Transport Features
sections.content:
The minimal set is divided into two main categories: Connection Management and Data Transfer.

Connection Management includes creating and configuring a connection before use; listening for incoming connections or actively connecting to a peer; specifying timeouts, retry limits, and notification preferences; and terminating connections with optional notification to the peer. Grouped connections support configuration of timeouts, scheduling urgency, and buffer drain notifications. Individual connections can configure per-message priorities and checksum behavior.

Data Transfer allows applications to send messages with choices about reliability (fully reliable, unreliable, or partially reliable), ordering (ordered or unordered), bundling (whether to bundle multiple messages), and whether to mark messages as idempotent (okay to deliver multiple times). On the receiving side, applications get an Application-Framed Byte Stream: a stream of bytes that respects message boundaries only if the sender specified them, and may contain reordered or missing data if the sender requested those options.
sections.plainLanguage: You set up a connection with timing and group information, then send messages with options about reliability and ordering, and receive back a stream of bytes that respects the choices you made.

sections.title: Implementation and Compatibility
sections.content:
The minimal set can be implemented directly over native TCP, with one limitation: TCP does not natively support message delimiting on the receiver side. To work around this, the Application-Framed Byte Stream approach requires the receiving application to determine message boundaries itself using knowledge from an application-layer protocol, such as a header with a length field or byte stuffing methods.

The minimal set can also be implemented one-sided over UDP: a UDP sender can use the interface, and a standard UDP receiver understands the resulting packets. However, the set is more restrictive over UDP because UDP does not support reliability, ordering, or notification of closing events.

The set includes optional features that may return errors if not available: per-message fragmentation preferences, buffer drain notifications, and maximum message size queries. Transport systems are not required to support all optional features, but must declare clearly what they do and do not support.
sections.plainLanguage: The design works on old protocols like TCP and UDP, even if TCP cannot do everything perfectly. If a transport system cannot do something, it can say so instead of silently failing.
